title: How Telescopes Work
keyIdea: A telescope is an instrument that helps us see distant objects in space. Its wide lens or curved mirror catches far more light than your eye, so faint stars and galaxies show up: the light caught grows with the area of the opening. A convex lens bends (refracts) the starlight and a concave mirror reflects it, so the light meets at one point, the focus, and an eyepiece lens magnifies the image. Moving air makes stars twinkle and blurs the view, so space telescopes work above the air: Hubble orbits Earth about 500 km up, and James Webb orbits the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth.
familyTip: On a clear night, look at the sky together for ten minutes and count the stars you can see near one bright star. Then look through binoculars, which are two small telescopes side by side: how many more can you count? Look for twinkling stars low in the sky, where the light passes through more air, and compare them with stars high overhead.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: widen a lens to find a faint galaxy, focus two lenses, pick the mirror that focuses light, and lift a telescope above the air.

kid: A telescope helps us see things that are very far away in space. Your eye has a tiny hole to let light in. A telescope has a much wider lens or mirror, so it catches far more light. Faint stars that you cannot see with your eyes show up.

Light from a star comes in straight. A curved glass lens bends the light, so it all meets at one point. That point is called the focus. Big telescopes use a curved mirror, shaped like a bowl, to bounce the light to a focus instead.
You look through a small lens called the eyepiece. It makes the picture look bigger. Move it to the right place and a blurry blob turns into a sharp dot.

The air around Earth is always moving. It bends starlight about, so stars twinkle and pictures blur. That is why some telescopes are sent into space. Hubble goes round Earth about 500 km up. James Webb is much farther away, past the Moon.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This supports 'Earth and space' in the National Curriculum in England (Year 5) and the light units in Year 3 and Year 6, and Next Generation Science Standards 1-PS4-3 and 4-PS4-2 on light. Facts were checked against NASA Space Place, the ESA/Hubble and NASA Webb fact sheets, and Royal Museums Greenwich. Key words: telescope, lens, mirror, focus, eyepiece, magnify, reflect, refract, atmosphere.

The lab has five tasks. Children widen a lens step by step and see that the light caught is width × width, so a 7 cm lens catches 49 times as much as a 1 cm lens and a faint galaxy appears; drag a screen to the focus of a thin and a fat lens; slot a flat, curved-in or bulging mirror into a reflecting telescope; lift a telescope from the ground to a mountain, plane height and Hubble's orbit; then judge three classmates.

Common mistakes. Children often think a telescope's main job is to make stars bigger (stars stay points; the wide opening is for collecting light), that stars twinkle because they switch on and off, that Hubble is in space to be nearer the stars, that any mirror will focus light, or that James Webb orbits Earth like Hubble. Be careful with the last one: Webb orbits the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth. Hubble was launched in 1990 and Webb on 25 December 2021.

practice.prompt: Why does a telescope show stars that your eyes cannot see?
choices: Its wide lens or mirror catches more light
It makes the stars shine brighter
It moves you closer to the stars
practice.hint: Think about the faint galaxy in the lab. What changed when it appeared?
practice.explain: A wider opening catches more light, so faint things show up. The stars themselves do not change.

practice.prompt: A lens {d} cm wide catches {d} × {d} times the light of a 1 cm lens. How many times is that?
practice.explain: {d} × {d} = {=d*d}, so it catches {=d*d} times the light. Twice as wide catches four times the light.

practice.prompt: What does a curved glass lens do to starlight?
choices: Bends it so it meets at one point
practice.hint: In the lab, where did the light lines meet?
practice.explain: A curved lens bends (refracts) the light so it meets at one point, called the focus.

practice.prompt: Telescope A has a mirror {a} m wide. Telescope B has a mirror {=2*a} m wide. How many times more light does B catch?
practice.hint: Light caught is width × width. What happens to width × width when the width doubles?
practice.explain: {=2*a} × {=2*a} = {=4*a*a}, and {a} × {a} = {=a*a}. {=4*a*a} ÷ {=a*a} = 4, so twice as wide catches 4 times the light.

practice.hint: What changed when you lifted the telescope above the air?
practice.explain: Stars shine steadily. Moving air in our sky bends their light about, so they seem to flicker. Above the air, they stop twinkling.

pool.prompt: Why is the Hubble Space Telescope in space?
choices: To get above the air that blurs the view
To be closer to the stars
Because telescopes do not work on Earth
pool.hint: What made the star twinkle in the lab?
pool.explain: The air blurs and bends starlight. About 500 km up, Hubble is above the air, so its pictures are sharp.

pool.prompt: Which mirror shape can bring starlight to one point?
pool.hint: Which mirror made the light meet in the lab?
pool.explain: A mirror curved in like a bowl bounces the light to one point. A flat one keeps it spread out, and a bulging one spreads it wider.

pool.prompt: What is the eyepiece of a telescope for?
choices: You look through it and it makes the picture bigger
It keeps dust out of the tube
pool.hint: It is the small lens next to your eye.
pool.explain: The eyepiece is a small lens that magnifies the picture made by the big lens or mirror.

pool.prompt: A lens is {d} cm wide. How many times the light of a 1 cm lens does it catch?
Where is the James Webb Space Telescope?
choices: In space, about 1.5 million km from Earth
On top of a high mountain
Going round Earth, just above the clouds
pool.hint: It is much farther away than Hubble, past the Moon.
pool.explain: Webb goes round the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth, about four times as far as the Moon.

pool.prompt: A star looks like a big blurry blob through a telescope. What is wrong?
pool.hint: In the lab, what turned the blob into a sharp dot?
pool.explain: The light is not meeting at your eye. Move the eyepiece until the blob shrinks to a sharp dot.

pool.prompt: Sam says, 'A telescope's big lens is there to make the stars look bigger.' What is the main job of the big lens?
pool.hint: Think about how the faint galaxy appeared.
pool.explain: The big lens or mirror catches light, so faint things show. The eyepiece does the magnifying.

pool.prompt: Why are many big telescopes built on high mountains?
choices: There is less air above them to blur the view
They are much nearer the stars there
Mountains are always sunny at night
pool.hint: What happened to the star at the mountain level in the lab?
pool.explain: Higher up there is less moving air above, so stars blur and twinkle less.

pool.prompt: What did Galileo see with his telescope in 1610?
choices: The first photo of a galaxy
pool.hint: He looked at the biggest planet.
pool.explain: In January 1610 Galileo saw four moons going round Jupiter. Photos and space telescopes came much later.

pool.prompt: Mirror A is {a} m wide. Mirror B is {=3*a} m wide. How many times as much light does mirror B catch?
pool.hint: Light caught is width × width. Work out width × width for each mirror, then divide.
pool.explain: {=3*a} × {=3*a} = {=9*a*a} and {a} × {a} = {=a*a}. {=9*a*a} ÷ {=a*a} = 9, so three times as wide catches 9 times the light.
